scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Once a high-status art used to teach noblemen etiquette, Mujra is a dance of 'asymmetry' where one woman commands a room of many men through poetry, song, and the refined gestures of Kathak.
This is Mujra. 16th to 19th century (Mughal era) to present.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (Uqjxz1Mraic)
Title card: Mujra · India; Pakistan · 16th to 19th century (Mughal era) to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Mujra emerged during Mughal rule in the Indian subcontinent as a performance for the elite class and nawabs.
It was traditionally a family art passed from mother to daughter in cultural centers like Delhi, Lucknow, and Lahore.
Tawaifs, or courtesans, were the primary practitioners and were often considered authorities on etiquette and culture, sometimes likened to Japanese geishas.
on_screen: Map: India; Pakistan · South Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically, tawaifs were invited to perform at significant events such as marriages or the birth of a male heir.
The dance signifies a 'payment of respects' or a 'deferential salute.' In the modern era, it is performed at weddings, birthdays, and bachelor parties.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Bharat Ek Khoj, Supplement 39 (https://archive.org/details/HindSwaraj-BEK-S39)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance combines elements of classical Kathak with sophisticated gestures.
It is described as elegant and artistic, often involving the dancer being the center of public eye for long periods.
The term 'mujra' itself refers to a deferential salute or payment of respects, which is reflected in the opening and closing movements of the performance.
Watch for Mujra.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (Uqjxz1Mraic)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Solo performance in a salon (kotha) or gathering (mehfil).

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The performance is set to Hindustani classical music, specifically genres like thumri and ghazal.
It incorporates poetry from the Mughal period, including works from the reigns of Akbar to Bahadur Shah Zafar.
Listen for the Tabla, Sarangi, Harmonium.

A blend of Hindustani classical music featuring melodic thumris and ghazals. The sound is characterized by poetic vocals and traditional instrumentation that supports a medium of exchange between the performer and the audience.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Traditionally performed in mehfils (intimate gatherings) or kothas (special houses/salons).
In historical contexts like Lahore's Heera Mandi, these settings were hubs for musicians and dancers.
Costumes are typically artistic and feminine, designed to make the dancer appear fluent and elegant.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The sources mention tawaifs as a class of performers who were authorities on culture.
In cinema, the dance is associated with characters like Umrao Jaan.
The performers are known by different names across the subcontinent: tawaifs in North India and Pakistan, baijis in Bengal, and naikins in Goa.
Mujra is a subclass of Asian dance and a derivative of the classical Kathak tradition.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Mujra is parent of Kathak: Mujra consolidates elements of classical Kathak dance into its performance.
Mujra is variant of Nautch: During the British colonial period, tawaifs were often referred to as Nautch girls.
